summary: Defines the Extensible Authentication Protocol, a framework that supports many authentication methods. It usually runs directly over link layers such as PPP or IEEE 802, without IP, and handles its own retransmission. It obsoletes RFC 2284 and was updated by RFC 5247 and RFC 7057.

plainLanguage.summary: Before you may join a network, you often have to prove who you are. EAP is a flexible envelope that can carry many different ways of proving it. The device that wants access answers questions from the network, and at the end the network says yes or no. The real checking can happen on a trusted server in the back office, so the access point itself does not need to understand every method.

subtitle: A flexible envelope that lets a network ask a device to prove who it is, using almost any authentication method.

tldr.problem: Networks need to authenticate devices before granting access, often on links where IP is not available yet, and they do not want to rebuild every switch or access point each time a new authentication method appears.
tldr.mechanism: EAP is a lock-step Request and Response exchange. The authenticator asks, the peer answers, and the conversation ends with a Success or Failure packet. The actual authentication logic lives in separate methods, which may run on a backend server while the authenticator just passes packets through.
tldr.outcome: RFC 3748 is a Proposed Standard that obsoletes RFC 2284 and has been updated by RFC 5247 and RFC 7057; no RFC obsoletes it. EAP leaves security to its methods, so every method specification must state its own security claims.

today: RFC 3748 is a Proposed Standard published in June 2004. It obsoletes RFC 2284 and has been updated by RFC 5247 and RFC 7057; no RFC obsoletes it.

sections.title: What EAP Is For
sections.content:
The Extensible Authentication Protocol (EAP) is an authentication framework that supports multiple authentication methods. It typically runs directly over data link layers such as the Point-to-Point Protocol (PPP) or IEEE 802, without requiring IP. It provides its own duplicate elimination and retransmission, but it relies on the lower layer to deliver packets in order. EAP itself does not fragment packets, although individual methods may.

EAP selects a specific authentication mechanism, typically after the authenticator asks for more information. Instead of updating the authenticator for every new method, a backend authentication server can implement the methods while the authenticator acts as a pass-through. Separating the two simplifies credentials management and policy decisions.

The RFC limits the scope on purpose. EAP was designed for network access authentication, where IP connectivity may not be available. Using it for other purposes such as bulk data transport is NOT RECOMMENDED, because it is a lock-step protocol with a single packet in flight.
sections.plainLanguage: EAP is like a doorman who does not check IDs himself. He passes a note to a helper who knows how to check many kinds of ID, and then lets you in or turns you away.

sections.title: The Request and Response Conversation
sections.content:
Three roles appear throughout. The authenticator is the end of the link that starts authentication. The peer is the end that responds (IEEE 802.1X calls it the Supplicant). The EAP server is the entity that ends the authentication method with the peer, which is either the authenticator itself or a backend server.

The exchange runs in steps. The authenticator sends a Request with a Type field, such as Identity or MD5-Challenge. The peer sends a Response of the matching Type. Requests and Responses continue as long as needed. EAP is lock-step: apart from the first Request, a new Request cannot be sent before a valid Response arrives. The conversation ends when the authenticator sends a Success (Code 3) or a Failure (Code 4). The authenticator MUST NOT send Success or Failure when it is merely retransmitting or when it gets no response from the peer.

An initial Identity Request is typical but not required; the identity may already be known from the port, the calling station identity or the MAC address. A conversation MAY use a sequence of methods, but only one authentication method (Type 4 or greater) may be used, after which the authenticator MUST send Success or Failure. Multiple methods are not supported because of their vulnerability to man-in-the-middle attacks. A tunneled method, which runs other methods inside one, appears to EAP as a single method and is exempt, but it MUST protect against man-in-the-middle attacks.
sections.plainLanguage: It is a game of question and answer where the doorman asks one question at a time and waits for your answer before asking the next. At the end he says either "come in" or "no entry".

sections.title: Layers, Pass-Through and Peer-to-Peer
sections.content:
The RFC describes an EAP implementation as four layers: the lower layer that carries EAP frames, the EAP layer that handles duplicate detection and retransmission, the EAP peer and authenticator layers, and the EAP method layers. An implementation does not have to follow this model as long as the on-the-wire behavior is consistent with it.

The Code field works much like a protocol number in IP: Requests, Successes and Failures go to the peer layer, and Responses go to the authenticator layer. The Type field works much like a port number in UDP or TCP, steering a packet to the right method. Success, Failure, Nak and Notification messages MUST NOT carry data destined for other methods.

In pass-through mode, the authenticator forwards Responses to the backend server and forwards Requests, Successes and Failures back to the peer, normally deciding only from the Code, Identifier and Length fields. A compliant pass-through authenticator MUST by default forward packets of any Type, and it MUST decide the outcome only from the Accept or Reject indication from the backend server, not from any encapsulated EAP packet. RADIUS and Diameter support only pass-through authenticator operation; the behavior of a "pass-through peer" is undefined and unsupported.

EAP is also peer-to-peer: both ends may act as authenticator and peer at the same time, if the lower layer and the methods support it. The RFC lists reasons why two authentications, one in each direction, can still be needed, such as lower layers that only support one-way key derivation.
sections.plainLanguage: The doorman can check a few IDs himself, but for most visitors he just walks the paperwork to the office in the back and does whatever the office says.

sections.title: What EAP Expects From the Link Below
sections.content:
EAP makes several assumptions about its lower layer. It does not assume the lower layer is reliable, because the authenticator retransmits unanswered Requests. It does rely on lower layer error detection such as a CRC, checksum or MIC, since methods may not protect every header field. It can function when the lower layer provides an EAP MTU of 1020 octets or greater, and methods can assume that minimum. Methods that may exceed it SHOULD support fragmentation and reassembly themselves; if the lower layer can fragment, giving EAP an artificially large MTU so the lower layer does the work may be preferable.

EAP does not require the Identifier to increase, so it depends on the lower layer to preserve ordering. Reordering will typically cause an authentication failure and a re-run. Running EAP over raw IP or UDP is NOT RECOMMENDED, while encapsulation within RADIUS satisfies the ordering requirement, because RADIUS is itself a lock-step protocol that delivers packets in order.

Within PPP, exactly one EAP packet is carried in a frame whose protocol field is hex C227, and EAP is negotiated through the Authentication Protocol Configuration Option, which lets the specific mechanism be chosen later in the Authentication Phase. Within IEEE 802, the encapsulation comes from IEEE 802.1X and involves no PPP, so non-EAP mechanisms such as PAP or CHAP cannot be negotiated.

Retransmission is the authenticator's job. Where the lower layer is unreliable, the timer SHOULD be estimated dynamically and a maximum of 3-5 retransmissions is suggested. Over a reliable lower layer the timer SHOULD be set to an infinite value so no retransmission happens at the EAP layer. Success and Failure packets are never retransmitted.
sections.plainLanguage: The doorman's notes must arrive in the order they were written and not be smudged on the way. EAP trusts the road for that, but it will repeat a question if no answer comes back.

sections.title: The EAP Packet
sections.content:
Every EAP packet starts with three fields: Code (one octet), Identifier (one octet) and Length (two octets, covering the whole EAP packet including Code, Identifier, Length and Data), followed by Data. The Codes are 1 Request, 2 Response, 3 Success and 4 Failure. Packets with any other Code MUST be silently discarded by both authenticators and peers. Octets beyond the Length are treated as link layer padding and ignored, while a packet whose Length is larger than the octets received MUST be silently discarded.

Request and Response packets add a one-octet Type and variable Type-Data. The Identifier matches a Response to its Request. Retransmitted Requests MUST keep the same Identifier, while any new Request MUST change it. A Response whose Identifier does not match the outstanding Request MUST be silently discarded. If a peer receives a valid duplicate Request for which it has already sent a Response, it MUST resend its original Response without reprocessing the Request. Initializing the first Identifier with a random number rather than zero is recommended, since it makes sequence attacks somewhat more difficult.

Success and Failure packets are only four octets long, carry no Type and MUST NOT contain additional data. Because they are not acknowledged, they are not retransmitted and may be lost. A peer MUST silently discard a "canned" Success sent immediately on connection, so a rogue authenticator cannot skip mutual authentication by sending Success before the method finishes.
sections.plainLanguage: Every EAP note has a little header saying what kind of note it is, which question it belongs to and how long it is. The final "yes" or "no" note is only the header itself.

sections.title: Method Types and Negotiation
sections.content:
The Type field says what a Request or Response is about. The first three are special: Identity (1) asks who the peer is, Notification (2) conveys a displayable message from the authenticator, and Nak (3) is valid only in a Response. The RFC also defines MD5-Challenge (4), One Time Password (5) and Generic Token Card (6). All implementations MUST support Types 1-4 and SHOULD support Type 254. Type 255 is for experimental use.

The Identity Response is recommended mainly for routing and for choosing a method, because Identity exchanges are sent in cleartext and an attacker may snoop, modify or spoof them. MD5-Challenge is analogous to PPP CHAP. The RFC does not define a cleartext password method on purpose; cleartext passwords could be captured by anyone with access to the link.

Methods are negotiated with the Nak. If the peer cannot accept the requested Type, it replies with a Nak listing the Types it would accept, one octet per Type, or a zero to say it has no viable alternative. A peer MUST NOT send a Nak after it has already sent a non-Nak Response. An Expanded Nak (Type 254) does the same job for Expanded Types, which add a 3-octet Vendor-Id and a 4-octet Vendor-Type; a Vendor-Id of 0 is reserved for the IETF and extends the global method Type space.

Because Nak packets are unprotected, an attacker may try to convince the peer and authenticator to negotiate a less secure method. The RFC's advice is that each named peer SHOULD have exactly one method used to authenticate it; if different methods are needed in different circumstances, distinct identities SHOULD be used.
sections.plainLanguage: If the doorman asks for one kind of ID and you do not have it, you answer "I have these other kinds instead". Some visitors carry special ID cards that only one company issues.

sections.title: Key Derivation
sections.content:
A method that supports key derivation MUST export a Master Session Key (MSK) of at least 64 octets and an Extended Master Session Key (EMSK) of at least 64 octets, and it MUST provide mutual authentication between peer and server. The MSK and EMSK MUST NOT be used directly to protect data. They are large enough to derive an AAA-Key, from which Transient Session Keys are derived for the ciphersuite chosen to protect subsequent data.

The EMSK is reserved for future use. It MUST remain on the EAP peer and EAP server and MUST NOT be transported to, or shared with, other parties. Methods SHOULD ensure freshness even when one party lacks a high quality random number generator; a RECOMMENDED way is for each party to provide a nonce of at least 128 bits. Methods SHOULD be capable of an effective key strength of at least 128 bits, and the MSK and EMSK branches must be cryptographically separate, so recovering one does not help recover the other without brute force. Methods SHOULD reuse well established mechanisms such as those in IKE or TLS rather than inventing new ones.

When the authenticator and the authentication server are separate machines, authentication happens between the peer and the server, not the authenticator, so the peer cannot validate the authenticator's identity with EAP alone. The AAA protocol between authenticator and server MUST support per-packet authentication, integrity and replay protection, because the authenticator learns the outcome only from that protocol. A secure association protocol SHOULD then run between peer and authenticator to bind the derived keys to the data that follows.
sections.plainLanguage: When the ID check is done, the two sides can also agree on a master secret code. They never use that master code directly. They use it to make fresh secret codes for the actual conversation afterwards.

sections.title: Threats and Security Claims
sections.content:
EAP assumes an attacker may reach the link. The threat list includes snooping identities, modifying or spoofing packets, denial of service through spoofed Success or Failure packets or replayed packets, offline dictionary attacks, man-in-the-middle attacks, forcing a weak method through negotiation, recovering keys from weak derivation, abusing weak ciphersuites after authentication, and a dishonest authenticator providing incorrect information to the peer or server. Over wireless and Internet links these attacks may be carried out without physical proximity.

Because the EAP layer itself provides no per-packet protection, the RFC requires every EAP method specification to include a Security Claims section. It states the authentication mechanism, the claimed properties (mutual authentication, integrity protection, replay protection, confidentiality, key derivation, dictionary attack resistance, fast reconnect, cryptographic binding), the effective key strength, the key hierarchy, and which claims are NOT made.

Several specific risks get their own treatment. Tunneling EAP inside a protocol that does not authenticate the peer allows a rogue authenticator to tunnel to a legitimate server and become a man-in-the-middle; mutual authentication within the tunnel and cryptographic binding are the main mitigations. One-way methods such as EAP-MD5 leave the peer open to rogue authenticators. Compromised pass-through authenticators can give the peer misleading information, which channel binding is meant to detect by comparing channel properties exchanged inside the method with those learned out of band. Success and Failure packets are neither acknowledged nor integrity protected, so methods can provide protected result indications to reduce the damage of losing or forging them.
sections.plainLanguage: Bad guys might listen in, send fake notes or trick the doorman into using the weakest check. So every kind of ID check has to publish a list of what it protects against and what it does not.

messages.label: Request (Type Identity)
messages.note: Typical first Request; it MAY be bypassed when the identity is known another way.

messages.label: Request (authentication Type)
messages.note: One authentication method only (Type 4 or greater); lock-step, no new Request before a valid Response.

messages.label: Response (matching Type)
messages.note: Or a Nak listing acceptable Types if the requested Type is unacceptable.

messages.label: Success (Code 3) or Failure (Code 4)
messages.note: Sent only after the method finishes; never sent while retransmitting or after a timeout.

layers.label: EAP methods
layers.detail: Implement the authentication algorithms; selected by the Type field

layers.label: EAP peer and authenticator layers
layers.detail: Split incoming packets by Code; Requests, Success, Failure go to the peer layer, Responses to the authenticator layer

layers.label: Lower layer
layers.detail: PPP, IEEE 802 (802.1X), and others carry the EAP frames

fields.name: Code
fields.desc: 1 Request, 2 Response, 3 Success, 4 Failure. Other codes are silently discarded.

fields.name: Identifier
fields.desc: Matches Responses to Requests; unchanged on retransmission, changed on each new Request.

fields.name: Length
fields.desc: Length of the whole EAP packet in octets; Success and Failure always have Length 4.

items.label: Identity
items.desc: Asks who the peer is; sent in cleartext, recommended mainly for routing.

items.label: Notification
items.desc: Displayable message from the authenticator; not an error indication.

items.label: Nak
items.desc: Response only; lists acceptable Types, or 0 for no alternative.

items.label: One Time Password (OTP)
items.desc: Works with the one-time password system.

items.label: Expanded Types
items.desc: Vendor-specific and expanded IETF Type space; includes the Expanded Nak.
